src.text:
INTRODUCTION (what the novel is, who wrote it, when):
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy is a 1979 science fiction comedy novel by English author Douglas Adams, adapted from the first four parts of his radio comedy series of the same name. It centres on the misadventures of Arthur Dent, the only man to survive the destruction of Earth, as he roams the cosmos and learns the truth behind his very existence. The novel's namesake is an in-universe electronic travel guide written in the form of an encyclopaedia, through which the story is framed.
The book was first published in London through Pan Books on 12 October 1979. It sold 250,000 copies in the first three months and is often regarded as a classic of the science fiction genre. It is the first in the "trilogy of six" Hitchhiker's Guide book series, with the second novel, The Restaurant at the End of the Universe, being published in 1980.

PLOT (an editor-reviewed concise summary of the whole story, 878 words; the ONLY source of the events):
The novel opens with an introduction describing the human race as a primitive and deeply unhappy species, while also introducing an electronic encyclopedia called the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy which provides information on every planet in the galaxy. 
Earthman and Englishman Arthur Dent awakens in his home in the West Country to discover that the local planning council is trying to demolish his house to build a bypass, and lies down in front of the bulldozer to stop it. His friend Ford Prefect convinces the lead bureaucrat to lie down in Arthur's stead so that he can take Arthur to the local pub. The construction crew begin demolishing the house anyway, but are interrupted by the sudden arrival of a fleet of spaceships. The Vogons, the callous race of civil servants running the fleet, announce that they have come to demolish Earth to make way for a hyperspace expressway, and promptly destroy the planet. Ford and Arthur survive by hitching a ride on the spaceship, much to Arthur's amazement. Ford reveals to Arthur he is an alien researcher for the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, from a small planet in the vicinity of Betelgeuse who has been posing as an out-of-work actor from Guildford for 15 years, and this was why they were able to hitch a ride on the alien ship. They are quickly discovered by the Vogons, who torture them by forcing them to listen to their poetry and then toss them out of an airlock.
Meanwhile, Zaphod Beeblebrox, Ford's "semi-cousin" and the President of the Galaxy, steals the spaceship Heart of Gold at its unveiling with his human companion, Trillian. The Heart of Gold is equipped with an "Infinite Improbability Drive" that allows it to travel instantaneously to any point in space by simultaneously passing through every point in the universe at once. However, the Infinite Improbability Drive has a side effect of causing impossible coincidences to occur in the physical universe. One of these improbable events occurs when Arthur and Ford are rescued by the Heart of Gold as it travels using the Infinite Improbability Drive. 
Zaphod takes his passengers—Arthur, Ford, a depressed robot named Marvin, and Trillian—to a legendary planet named Magrathea. Its inhabitants were said to have specialized in custom-building planets for others and to have vanished after becoming so rich that the rest of the galaxy became poor. Although Ford initially doubts that the planet is Magrathea, the planet's computers send them warning messages to leave before firing two nuclear missiles at the Heart of Gold. Arthur inadvertently saves them by activating the Infinite Improbability Drive improperly, which also opens an underground passage. As the ship lands, Trillian's pet mice Frankie and Benjy escape.
On Magrathea, Zaphod, Ford, and Trillian venture down to the planet's interior while leaving Arthur and Marvin outside. In the tunnels, Zaphod reveals that his actions are not a result of his own decisions, but instead motivated by neural programming that he was seemingly involved in but has no memory of. As Zaphod explains how he discovered this, the trio are trapped and knocked out with sleeping gas. On the surface, Arthur is met by a resident of Magrathea, a man named Slartibartfast, who explains that the Magratheans have been in stasis to wait out an economic recession. They have temporarily reawakened to reconstruct a second version of Earth commissioned by mice, who were in fact the most intelligent species on Earth. Slartibartfast brings Arthur to Magrathea's planet construction facility, and shows Arthur that in the distant past, a race of "hyperintelligent, pan-dimensional beings" created a supercomputer named Deep Thought to determine the answer to the "Ultimate Question to Life, the Universe, and Everything." Deep Thought eventually found the answer to be 42, an answer that made no sense because the Ultimate Question itself was not known. Because determining the Ultimate Question was too difficult even for Deep Thought, an even more advanced supercomputer was constructed for this purpose. This computer was the planet Earth, which was constructed by the Magratheans, and was five minutes away from finishing its task and figuring out the Ultimate Question when the Vogons destroyed it. The hyperintelligent superbeings participated in the program as mice, performing experiments on humans while pretending to be experimented on.
Slartibartfast takes Arthur to see his friends, who are at a feast hosted by Trillian's pet mice. The mice reject as unnecessary the idea of building a new Earth to start the process over, deciding that Arthur's brain likely contains the Ultimate Question. They offer to buy Arthur's brain, leading to a fight when he declines. The group manages to escape when the planet's security system goes off unexpectedly, but immediately run into the culprits: police in pursuit of Zaphod. The police corner Zaphod, Arthur, Ford and Trillian, and the situation seems desperate as they are trapped behind a computer bank that is about to explode from the officers' weapons firing. However, the police officers suddenly die when their life-support systems short-circuit. Suspicious, Ford discovers on the surface that Marvin became bored and explained his view of the universe to the police officers' spaceship, causing it to commit suicide. The five leave Magrathea and decide to go to The Restaurant at the End of the Universe.

SIGNIFICANCE (themes, reception, legacy: use ONLY for the closing wrap-up, to say why the novel matters):
[Reception]
Greg Costikyan reviewed The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy in Ares Magazine #6 and commented that "The Hitchhiker's Guide is written with superb English wit, far more humorous than any American sitcom." The Pequod rated the book a 9.5 (out of 10.0) and called it "an ingeniously silly sci-fi satire... It may not add up to much but the jokes keep coming fast and furiously and its enormous cultural influence ("Don't Panic," etc.) proves to be well-earned."
C. J. Henderson reviewed The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy for Pegasus magazine and stated that "It is silly, happy, absurd stuff. It is the wildest funniest, sci fi novel ever. The only disappointing thing about it is that the reader is forced to wait for the next volume to come out to get more of the same."

[Legacy]
The "Babel fish", a creature used in the novel that feeds on brainwaves and can instantly translate alien languages, inspired the name of Babel Fish, the first free online language translator, which launched in 1997.
Radiohead's song "Paranoid Android" (1997) was named after Marvin's nickname, and the album it appears on, OK Computer, is part of a line spoken by Zaphod to Eddie, the Heart of Gold's computer.
The Trillian instant messaging app (2000–) was named after the character.

script.art_style_en: hand-drawn storybook illustration in the style of a gentle animated film, fine dark ink outlines, soft painterly colors, warm cozy lamplight and atmospheric weather, richly detailed backgrounds, natural proportions, expressive realistic faces, whole picture in this one style
script.era_en: Earth, late 1970s; Galactic space, timeless. Clothing of that time: Earth humans wear corduroy, wool, and cotton knits in muted earth tones. Aliens wear futuristic, synthetic materials, metallic fabrics, and complex, asymmetrical silhouettes that defy traditional terrestrial tailoring.

locations.name_en: Arthur's Home in the West Country
locations.detail_en: A quaint, slightly cluttered English cottage garden set in the rolling green hills of the West Country. The scene features a stone-walled house with ivy-covered brickwork and a manicured lawn. The atmosphere is peaceful, bathed in soft, overcast British sunlight. Essential to the events are the wooden garden bench where Arthur sits, the dirt path where the bulldozer idles, and the front door where Ford Prefect first arrives.

A sleek, ultra-modern vessel with a pristine white, curved interior that feels both organic and high-tech. The walls are polished chrome and glowing panels, illuminated by cold blue LED strips. Key features include the central control console where Zaphod stands, the plush, gravity-defying lounge area for the passengers, and the complex, humming housing unit of the Infinite Improbability Drive that anchors the ship's mysterious, reality-bending power source.

A desolate, frozen wasteland with vast, jagged crystalline structures protruding from the icy ground. The sky is a deep, bruised purple, lit by the dim light of a dying sun. The landscape feels ancient and forgotten. Necessary for the story are the hidden elevator entrance leading to the subterranean tunnels, the desolate landing pad for the ship, and the metallic security terminal that triggers the planet's defensive weaponry.

A colossal, cavernous industrial complex located deep within the planet's crust, filled with giant, ancient gears and glowing computer banks. The architecture is brutalist and imposing, featuring dark metallic walkways and pipes that stretch into darkness. Essential locations include the central observation platform where the history of Earth is displayed, the trap-door room where the gas release occurs, and the grand feast table where the mice hold their meeting.

outline.what_en: Ford convinces a bureaucrat to take Arthur's place lying in front of a bulldozer so Arthur can visit the local pub.
outline.where_en: Arthur's home and the local pub in the West Country
outline.quote_en: His friend Ford Prefect convinces the lead bureaucrat to lie down in Arthur's stead so that he can take Arthur to the local pub.

outline.what_en: A Vogon fleet arrives and demolishes planet Earth to make room for a hyperspace expressway.
outline.because_en: The demolition of Arthur's house is interrupted by the fleet's arrival to destroy the entire planet.
outline.quote_en: The construction crew begin demolishing the house anyway, but are interrupted by the sudden arrival of a fleet of spaceships.

outline.what_en: Arthur and Ford escape Earth's obliteration by hitching a ride aboard the Vogon spaceship.
outline.because_en: Earth's destruction forces Ford to use his alien background to hitch a ride to save their lives.
outline.quote_en: Ford and Arthur survive by hitching a ride on the spaceship, much to Arthur's amazement.

outline.what_en: The Vogons discover the stowaways, subject them to poetry torture, and eject them into open space.
outline.because_en: The Vogons discover Arthur and Ford aboard their vessel without authorization.
outline.quote_en: They are quickly discovered by the Vogons, who torture them by forcing them to listen to their poetry and then toss them out of an airlock.

outline.what_en: The Heart of Gold automatically rescues Arthur and Ford from the vacuum of space through an improbable coincidence.
outline.where_en: Aboard the Heart of Gold in space
outline.because_en: Being tossed out of the Vogon airlock leaves Arthur and Ford dying in open space.
outline.quote_en: One of these improbable events occurs when Arthur and Ford are rescued by the Heart of Gold as it travels using the Infinite Improbability Drive.

outline.who_en: Zaphod Beeblebrox, Arthur Dent, Ford Prefect, Trillian, and Marvin
outline.what_en: The Heart of Gold reaches the legendary planet Magrathea and comes under fire from its defense missiles.
outline.because_en: Zaphod pilots his newly assembled crew directly to the planet Magrathea.
outline.quote_en: Although Ford initially doubts that the planet is Magrathea, the planet's computers send them warning messages to leave before firing two nuclear missiles at the Heart of Gold.

outline.what_en: Arthur accidentally triggers the Infinite Improbability Drive, which neutralizes the missiles and reveals an entrance into Magrathea.
outline.because_en: Magrathea's automated missile defense threatens to destroy the incoming spaceship.
outline.quote_en: Arthur inadvertently saves them by activating the Infinite Improbability Drive improperly, which also opens an underground passage.

outline.who_en: Zaphod Beeblebrox, Ford Prefect, and Trillian
outline.what_en: Zaphod, Ford, and Trillian explore the interior tunnels of Magrathea and are knocked unconscious by sleeping gas.
outline.because_en: The passage opened by Arthur allows the trio to explore beneath the planet's surface.
outline.quote_en: As Zaphod explains how he discovered this, the trio are trapped and knocked out with sleeping gas.

outline.what_en: Slartibartfast reveals to Arthur that Magratheans are building a second Earth commissioned by hyperintelligent mice.
outline.where_en: Magrathea's surface and planet construction facility
outline.because_en: Arthur is left behind outside while his companions venture into the interior tunnels.
outline.quote_en: They have temporarily reawakened to reconstruct a second version of Earth commissioned by mice, who were in fact the most intelligent species on Earth.

outline.who_en: Trillian's pet mice and Arthur Dent
outline.what_en: The mice attempt to purchase Arthur's brain to extract the Ultimate Question, sparking a violent brawl when he refuses.
outline.because_en: Slartibartfast reunites Arthur with his friends at the feast hosted by the mice.
outline.quote_en: They offer to buy Arthur's brain, leading to a fight when he declines.

outline.who_en: Arthur Dent, Ford Prefect, Zaphod Beeblebrox, and Trillian
outline.what_en: The travelers flee the fight with the mice only to be pinned down under heavy gunfire from galactic police.
outline.because_en: The group escapes the mice during a sudden security alarm triggered by the arriving police.
outline.quote_en: The group manages to escape when the planet's security system goes off unexpectedly, but immediately run into the culprits: police in pursuit of Zaphod.

outline.what_en: Marvin's depressing conversation drives the police officers' spaceship to commit suicide, killing the pursuing officers.
outline.because_en: Marvin was left alone on the surface with nothing to do while the police ambushed the crew underground.
outline.quote_en: Suspicious, Ford discovers on the surface that Marvin became bored and explained his view of the universe to the police officers' spaceship, causing it to commit suicide.

outline.who_en: Arthur Dent, Ford Prefect, Zaphod Beeblebrox, Trillian, and Marvin
outline.what_en: The five companions leave Magrathea behind and set off together for The Restaurant at the End of the Universe.
outline.where_en: Departing Magrathea aboard the Heart of Gold
outline.because_en: The death of the police officers allows the reunited group to safely return to their ship and escape.
outline.quote_en: The five leave Magrathea and decide to go to The Restaurant at the End of the Universe.

spine.logline: After Earth is destroyed to make way for a hyperspace bypass, Arthur Dent wanders the cosmos with alien companions while trying to survive bizarre galactic threats and discover the truth of existence.

heroes.name: Arthur Dent
heroes.role_en: The only human man to survive the destruction of planet Earth.

heroes.name: Ford Prefect
heroes.role_en: Arthur's alien friend and field researcher for the galactic travel guide.

heroes.name: Zaphod Beeblebrox
heroes.role_en: Ford's semi-cousin and the runaway President of the Galaxy.

heroes.name: Trillian
heroes.role_en: A human woman traveling the cosmos as Zaphod's companion.

events.what_en: Ford convinces a bureaucrat to take Arthur's place lying in front of a bulldozer so Arthur can visit the local pub.
events.where_en: Arthur's home and the local pub in the West Country
events.quote_en: His friend Ford Prefect convinces the lead bureaucrat to lie down in Arthur's stead so that he can take Arthur to the local pub.

events.what_en: A Vogon fleet arrives and demolishes planet Earth to make room for a hyperspace expressway.
events.because_en: The demolition of Arthur's house is interrupted by the fleet's arrival to destroy the entire planet.
events.quote_en: The construction crew begin demolishing the house anyway, but are interrupted by the sudden arrival of a fleet of spaceships.

events.what_en: Arthur and Ford escape Earth's obliteration by hitching a ride aboard the Vogon spaceship.
events.because_en: Earth's destruction forces Ford to use his alien background to hitch a ride to save their lives.
events.quote_en: Ford and Arthur survive by hitching a ride on the spaceship, much to Arthur's amazement.

spine.ending_en: Arthur and his fellow space travelers leave Magrathea aboard the Heart of Gold to dine at The Restaurant at the End of the Universe.
spine.idea_en: It centres on the misadventures of Arthur Dent, the only man to survive the destruction of Earth, as he roams the cosmos and learns the truth behind his very existence.
spine.author_en: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy is a 1979 science fiction comedy novel by English author Douglas Adams, first published on 12 October 1979.
